chunks.x: The democratization of capability. A blind person can read a menu. A researcher in Lagos can access 200 million protein structures. A student in Guatemala can learn 42 languages for free. A weather forecast that used to cost a supercomputer now costs a GPU. These are genuine, measurable, life-improving goods.

chunks.pt: AI and Society: The Cultural Impact of Machines That Create
chunks.x: The parasocial shift. AI companions are not a fad. They are a new category of human experience — a one-sided relationship with a system that simulates the other side. The legal, ethical, and psychological frameworks for this are being built in real time, in courtrooms and in the bedrooms of teenagers.

chunks.pt: AI and Society: The Cultural Impact of Machines That Create
chunks.x: The cultural equilibrium we are forming is not "AI is good" or "AI is bad." It is: AI is a powerful, asymmetric, double-edged technology that amplifies whatever human intention is directed at it. It amplifies the scientist's curiosity and the criminal's greed. It amplifies the teacher's patience and the scammer's persi…

chunks.pt: AI and Society: The Cultural Impact of Machines That Create
chunks.x: The question that remains — the question that Dartmouth could not have answered, and that we are still asking — is not "can machines think?" It is: *what do we do with machines that can?*

chunks.pt: AI and Society: The Cultural Impact of Machines That Create
chunks.x: And the answer to that question is not a technical answer. It is a cultural one. It is written in the contracts we negotiate (the WGA, the licensing deals), the laws we pass (the EU AI Act, the FCC robocall ban, the deepfake labeling requirements), the defaults we choose (opt-in vs. opt-out, consent vs. scraping), and…

chunks.pt: AI and Society: The Cultural Impact of Machines That Create
chunks.x: The story is not over. It is, in every meaningful sense, just beginning.

chunks.pt: How Algorithms Work: From Euclid to the Transformer
chunks.x: You have used the word algorithm so many times it has lost all meaning. A sorting step is an algorithm. A search is an algorithm. The way your coffee machine cycles through its modes is, in the strict sense, an algorithm. But there is a question almost nobody asks, and it is the one this whole field was eventually buil…

chunks.pt: How Algorithms Work: From Euclid to the Transformer
chunks.x: It must terminate. An algorithm is not an infinite loop. It must finish, in a finite number of steps, for every input it promises to handle. It must be correct — by construction. Not "it usually works," not "we tested a few cases," but guaranteed right, by an argument that holds for every input.

chunks.pt: How Algorithms Work: From Euclid to the Transformer
chunks.x: A procedure that has both is an algorithm. The rest of this half is the story of those two properties — and of how, in a single decade, they went from being quietly practiced for two thousand years to being rigorously studied.

chunks.x: A few decades later, in Alexandria, the same two millennia-old craft produced a different shape of procedure: the Sieve of Eratosthenes. Given a limit n, list every number from 2 to n, then cross off every multiple of 2, then every multiple of 3, then 5, and so on. What is left standing is exactly the set of primes.

chunks.pt: How Algorithms Work: From Euclid to the Transformer
chunks.h: Another shape of algorithm: the Sieve of Eratosthenes (c. 240 BC)
chunks.x: Where Euclid's algorithm reduces a problem step by step, the sieve filters a finite set. It is still an algorithm, for the same two reasons: it terminates (once the smallest number you have not crossed off, p, satisfies p² > n, nothing below n can still be composite, so you are done), and it is correct by construction…

And yet they compute exactly the same set of functions — every problem one can solve, the other can solve too. That coincidence is so load-bearing that it has its own name: the Church–Turing thesis (SEP).

chunks.pt: How Algorithms Work: From Euclid to the Transformer
chunks.x: When we train a neural network on a simple task like modular addition, something remarkable happens. The network doesn't just memorize the answers, it discovers an algorithm. Specifically, it learns to use the Discrete Fourier Transform to convert addition into wave interference, as described by (Nanda et al., 2023).

chunks.pt: The Semantic Tug-of-War: How Transformers 'Think'
chunks.x: If Q and K have entries drawn from a distribution with mean 0 and variance 1, then their dot product Q · K = ∑ᵢ=₁dₖ qᵢ kᵢ has: Var(Q · K) = dₖ

chunks.pt: The Semantic Tug-of-War: How Transformers 'Think'
chunks.x: As the dimensionality dₖ increases, the standard deviation grows as √dₖ. Dividing by √dₖ normalizes the variance back to 1: Var(Q · K/√dₖ) = 1

chunks.pt: The Semantic Tug-of-War: How Transformers 'Think'
chunks.x: The “Aha!” Moment: Without this scaling, if dₖ = 64, your dot products would have a standard deviation of ~8. Applying Softmax over values spread across a wide range (like [-24, +24]) produces “near-one-hot” outputs, where one token gets ~100% of the weight and everything else gets ~0%. This causes gradients to vanish…

chunks.pt: The Semantic Tug-of-War: How Transformers 'Think'
chunks.x: The √dₖ division keeps scores in the “Goldilocks zone” where softmax produces soft distributions that gradients can flow through. It is the difference between asking “rate this restaurant 1–10” (useful) vs. “rate it 1–10,000,000” (where nuance is lost).

chunks.pt: The Semantic Tug-of-War: How Transformers 'Think'
chunks.x: But why this specific formula? Why dot products? Why softmax? Why √dₖ?

chunks.pt: The Semantic Tug-of-War: How Transformers 'Think'
chunks.x: Dot product QKᵀ: It's the natural measure of directional alignment. In 1D it's just multiplication (same sign = agree). In 2D/3D it's \\θ, the projection of one vector onto another. No other simple operation captures “how much do these vectors point the same way?”

chunks.pt: The Semantic Tug-of-War: How Transformers 'Think'
chunks.x: √dₖ scaling: Without it, as dₖ grows, the expected magnitude of dot products grows as √dₖ, pushing softmax toward hard one-hot outputs. The scaling keeps the variance of scores constant regardless of dimension, preserving smooth gradients.

chunks.pt: The Semantic Tug-of-War: How Transformers 'Think'
chunks.x: Softmax: Turns raw scores into a probability distribution, non-negative weights that sum to 1. This means the output is a convex combination of values, geometrically trapped inside their convex hull. It's the minimal assumption: “blend the available information proportionally to relevance.”

chunks.pt: The Semantic Tug-of-War: How Transformers 'Think'
chunks.x: Weighted sum of Values: The output is an interpolation, not a lookup. This is differentiable everywhere, enabling gradient-based learning. The FFN layer that follows provides the non-linearity needed to “escape” the convex hull and create genuinely new representations.

chunks.pt: The Semantic Tug-of-War: How Transformers 'Think'
chunks.x: There is a third reading of the same equation, from kernel methods. If you treat the softmax weights as a kernel over keys, attention can be read as Nadaraya–Watson kernel smoothing: the output at a query is a weighted average of the values, with weights that fall off as the query and key diverge (Tsai et al., 2019). T…

chunks.pt: The Semantic Tug-of-War: How Transformers 'Think'
chunks.x: Query (q): The word looking for context (e.g., “What kind of Bank am I?”). Key (k): The words offering context (e.g., “I am a River, I have water and banks.”). Value (v): The actual semantic “content” to be shared.

chunks.pt: The Semantic Tug-of-War: How Transformers 'Think'
chunks.x: The model calculates an alignment score using the scaled dot product: scoreᵢ,ⱼ = ᵢ · kⱼᵀ√dₖ The √dₖ term is critical, without it, the dot-product magnitudes scale with the head dimension and the softmax saturates. If the Query and Key point in a similar direction, the connection is strong.

chunks.pt: The Semantic Tug-of-War: How Transformers 'Think'
chunks.x: In modern NLP, words are not merely strings; they are high-dimensional vectors. Self-Attention is the operation that allows a model to dynamically re-weight these vectors based on their contextual relevance to one another.

chunks.pt: The Semantic Tug-of-War: How Transformers 'Think'
chunks.h: A Simple Picture: Attention Is Moving Sand
chunks.x: Imagine you have exactly one bucket of attention to hand out. The keys are places that can take some of it. Sending attention to a key that is very similar to the query is cheap; sending it to a very different key is expensive. So you naturally want to send the sand where it is cheap.

chunks.pt: The Semantic Tug-of-War: How Transformers 'Think'
chunks.h: A Simple Picture: Attention Is Moving Sand
chunks.x: But there is a catch. If you pour the whole bucket onto the single cheapest key, you commit completely. A tiny difference in similarity then decides everything, and the model stops listening to the other keys. To stay flexible, you also want to spread some sand around. These two wishes pull in opposite directions:

chunks.pt: The Semantic Tug-of-War: How Transformers 'Think'
chunks.h: A Simple Picture: Attention Is Moving Sand
chunks.x: Cheap: put the mass on the most similar key. Spread out: do not put all your eggs in one basket.

chunks.pt: The Semantic Tug-of-War: How Transformers 'Think'
chunks.h: A Simple Picture: Attention Is Moving Sand
chunks.x: The paper's central result is that this tug-of-war has one unique best answer, and that answer is exactly the softmax that attention already uses (Litman, 2025). The formula was not invented as a plausible trick; it is the solution to a precise problem.

chunks.pt: The Semantic Tug-of-War: How Transformers 'Think'
chunks.x: The size of the shares is controlled by the temperature τ. A small τ magnifies small score differences, so the plan becomes sharp. A large τ flattens the differences, so the plan becomes almost even. In a Transformer, the temperature is τ=√dₖ, a point we return to below.

chunks.pt: The Semantic Tug-of-War: How Transformers 'Think'
chunks.x: If two keys differ by Δ in score, the better one receives eᵗa/\ᵗau times more weight. The exponential is the natural way to turn a difference into a factor: adding the same constant to all scores does not change the plan, and the weights stay positive. That is exactly what a probability distribution needs.

chunks.pt: Automatic Differentiation: How Machines Learn
chunks.x: ReLU Activation (Vinod Nair, Geoffrey E. Hinton, 2010): The Rectified Linear Unit ReLU(z) = (0, z) has a derivative of exactly 1 for positive inputs, preventing the multiplicative shrinkage that plagues sigmoid networks.

chunks.pt: Automatic Differentiation: How Machines Learn
chunks.x: Residual Connections (Kaiming He, Xiangyu Zhang, Shaoqing Ren, Jian Sun, 2015): Skip connections add the input of a block directly to its output: y = F(x) + x. This creates a “gradient highway” that allows gradients to bypass problematic layers entirely.

chunks.pt: Automatic Differentiation: How Machines Learn
chunks.x: Layer Normalization (Jimmy Lei Ba, Jamie Ryan Kiros, Geoffrey Everest Hinton, 2016): Normalizing activations at each layer keeps their scale stable and makes optimization less sensitive to initialization; it helps with vanishing gradients but is not a guarantee against either failure mode.

chunks.x: Distinction. Before anything can be related, something has to be marked off from something else. chunks.pt: Coherent Difference
chunks.x: Gluing. When local pieces are coherent, they assemble into a unique global object. A sheaf is exactly a gadget whose global sections are determined by compatible local sections Wikipedia contributors, 2026.

chunks.pt: Coherent Difference
chunks.x: Globality. What looked like a patchwork of perspectives turns out to be one* thing, not because the patches are identical, but because their seams fit.

chunks.pt: Coherent Difference
chunks.x: Invariance. The result is no longer tied to any particular choice of cover or chart. It survives every legitimate change of viewpoint. This is what manifold, topological space, fiber bundle Wikipedia contributors, 2026, type, and object in a category all have in common.

chunks.pt: From World to Model: Coherent Representation
chunks.x: The world-level: W₁ ≠ W₂. Two subjects genuinely differ: two distinct stones, two historical events, two specific classical objects. Reports disagree because the world itself is different at the two accesses.

chunks.pt: From World to Model: Coherent Representation
chunks.x: Example. Alice weighs stone A; Bob weighs stone B (a different stone). Their data need not match, and the right response is not to reconcile them, but to note that they are about different things.

chunks.pt: From World to Model: Coherent Representation
chunks.x: Caveat. Identical quantum particles (electrons, photons) are literally indistinguishable: there is no fact of the matter about "this electron" versus "that electron", and asking whose data matches whose has no answer at the particle level. For such systems the world-level difference is the difference of spacetime regio…

chunks.pt: From World to Model: Coherent Representation
chunks.x: The channel-level: I₁ ≠ I₂. Two instruments read the same world differently: thermometer vs. thermocouple, eye vs. microphone, uncalibrated vs. calibrated telescope.

chunks.pt: From World to Model: Coherent Representation
chunks.x: Example. Two thermometers placed at the same point read 20.01 and 20.02. At that point the room has one temperature; the difference must be in the instruments: at least one, possibly both, is miscalibrated. The remedy is calibration against each other, against an external standard, or via a third instrument to adjudica…

chunks.pt: From World to Model: Coherent Representation
chunks.x: Co-location matters. If the thermometers are at different positions in a non-uniform temperature field (one near a window, one near a heater), they may legitimately report different values, and that would be a world-level difference (different points in the field), not a channel-level one.

chunks.pt: From World to Model: Coherent Representation
chunks.x: The processing-level: ν₁ ≠ ν₂. Two interpretations of the same trace yield different conclusions: a classical and a quantum reading of the same detector output, a literal and a metaphorical reading of the same text, an outdated and a current taxonomy applied to the same specimen.

chunks.pt: From World to Model: Coherent Representation
chunks.x: Example. The same Doppler-shifted spectrum is read by one physicist as evidence for a moving source, by another as evidence for an expanding universe. The trace is fixed; the interpretive framework differs.

chunks.pt: Differentiation: The Mathematics of Change
chunks.x: The concept of a derivative is one of the most important ideas in all of mathematics. It answers a deceptively simple question: How fast is something changing at this exact moment?

chunks.pt: Differentiation: The Mathematics of Change
chunks.x: If you drive a car and your speedometer reads 60 km/h, that number is a derivative, it tells you the instantaneous rate of change of your position with respect to time. But how do we define “instantaneous” mathematically, when an instant has zero duration?

chunks.pt: Differentiation: The Mathematics of Change
chunks.x: This question puzzled mathematicians for centuries, and its resolution gave birth to an entire branch of mathematics: Calculus.

chunks.pt: Differentiation: The Mathematics of Change
chunks.x: Gradient Descent: To train a neural network, we need to minimize a loss function that measures how wrong the model's predictions are. The derivative (or gradient, in multiple dimensions) tells us which direction to adjust the weights to reduce the loss. This is the algorithm called Gradient Descent, first described by…

chunks.pt: Differentiation: The Mathematics of Change
chunks.x: Backpropagation: As we saw, the chain rule allows us to compute the gradient of the loss with respect to every single weight in a deep network, no matter how many layers it has. This algorithm, popularized by David E. Rumelhart, Geoffrey E. Hinton, Ronald J. Williams in 1986, is what makes deep learning possible.

chunks.pt: Differentiation: The Mathematics of Change
chunks.x: Optimization Landscape: The derivative tells us about the “shape” of the loss function, where it slopes up, where it slopes down, and where it is flat (critical points). Understanding this landscape is key to training models effectively.

chunks.pt: Differentiation: The Mathematics of Change
chunks.x: The Sigmoid Derivative: As the table above shows, the sigmoid function σ(z) = 1/1+e⁻z has the elegant derivative σ'(z) = σ(z)(1-σ(z)). This means once you compute the forward pass, the backward pass is nearly free, you already have all the values you need.

chunks.pt: Differentiation: The Mathematics of Change
chunks.x: In summary, without derivatives, there would be no way to train neural networks, and modern AI as we know it would not exist.

chunks.pt: Differentiation: The Mathematics of Change
chunks.x: The derivative is the bridge between static mathematics and dynamic change. It is the tool that lets us ask “what happens next?” and, in the context of AI, “how should we adjust?” Without it, machines could not learn.

chunks.pt: Diffusion Models
chunks.x: Most of AI's image generators used to be delicate. GANs collapsed, VAEs blurred, and training them was an art. Then in 2020, a paper called DDPM (Ho et al., 2020) turned a 2015 idea from Jascha Sohl-Dickstein and colleagues (Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015) into a practical recipe: learn to reverse a fixed noising process.

chunks.pt: Diffusion Models
chunks.h: The central trick: destroy, then learn to undo
chunks.x: Imagine dropping a clear photograph into a glass of water and slowly stirring in drops of black ink. After each drop the picture becomes a little less recognizable. After enough drops, all you see is uniform grey.

chunks.pt: Diffusion Models
chunks.h: The central trick: destroy, then learn to undo
chunks.x: Now imagine the reverse: starting with grey water, learn to remove exactly the right amount of ink, drop by drop, until a coherent photograph reappears. If you can learn that reverse process well enough, you can start from any grey water and turn it into a fresh, novel photograph.

chunks.pt: Diffusion Models
chunks.h: The central trick: destroy, then learn to undo
chunks.x: That is what a diffusion model does. The forward process (ink going in) is a hand-designed procedure with no learned parameters. The reverse process (ink coming out) is what a neural network has to learn.

chunks.x: The text prompt goes through CLIP, the latent goes through the U-Net, and at the end a frozen VAE decoder turns the clean latent back into an image. The VAE is never trained alongside the diffusion model, it was learned earlier as an ordinary autoencoder and frozen in place.

chunks.pt: Diffusion Models
chunks.x: By 2025, many new systems use flow matching (Lipman et al., 2023) or its rectified-flow variant, in which the path between data and noise is trained to be straighter than the curved diffusion path. FLUX and Stable Diffusion 3 use rectified flow; DDPM/DDIM-style samplers remain widespread in older and distilled models.

chunks.pt: Diffusion Models
chunks.x: The dominant backbone is no longer the U-Net but the Diffusion Transformer (DiT) (Peebles & Xie, 2023), a vanilla Vision Transformer scaled up. Sora, FLUX, and Stable Diffusion 3 all use DiT-style backbones. The pattern is familiar: U-Net worked, then Transformers worked better once they were big enough.

chunks.pt: Diffusion Models
chunks.x: Practical models have also become fast. Modern systems generate images in 1–8 network evaluations through clever solvers (DPM-Solver, EDM) and adversarial distillation (SDXL-Turbo, LCM). Diffusion is no longer slow.

chunks.pt: Diffusion Models
chunks.x: In five years, the technique went from “diffusion as a curiosity” to “diffusion as the universal generative recipe” for images, video, audio, and molecules.

chunks.pt: Embeddings: The Geometry of Meaning
chunks.x: Riemann was attempting to generalize the idea of a surface to higher dimensions. Before Riemann, geometry was essentially limited to the study of curves (1D), surfaces (2D), and ordinary 3D Euclidean space. The key problems driving his work were:

chunks.pt: Embeddings: The Geometry of Meaning
chunks.x: Extending geometry beyond three dimensions: Riemann wanted a rigorous mathematical framework for spaces of any number of dimensions, not just the two-dimensional surfaces studied by Gauß.

chunks.pt: Embeddings: The Geometry of Meaning
chunks.x: Understanding spaces that are locally flat but globally complex: Manifolds are shapes that “look flat to an ant living on them, even though they might have a more complicated global structure.” A sphere, for example, looks flat if you're standing on it (like the Earth), but its global structure is curved and closed.

chunks.pt: Embeddings: The Geometry of Meaning
chunks.x: Describing the set of all possible values of a variable under constraints: Riemann described a Mannigfaltigkeit as the set of all possible values a variable can take when subject to certain constraints, he used the term precisely because “the variable can have many values.”

chunks.pt: Embeddings: The Geometry of Meaning
chunks.x: While Euclidean distance measures the physical gap between points, modern LLMs often rely on Cosine Similarity. This measures the cosine of the angle θ between two vectors, determining their directional alignment regardless of their magnitude. A similarity of 1 means the vectors point in the same direction.

chunks.pt: Embeddings: The Geometry of Meaning
chunks.x: The Dot Product has a beautiful geometric property: High Positive Number: The arrows point in roughly the same direction (They are “Similar”). Zero: The arrows are at a right angle (They are “Unrelated”). Negative Number: The arrows point in opposite directions (They are “Opposites”).

chunks.pt: Evaluation & Benchmarks
chunks.x: You cannot improve what you cannot measure. The evaluation problem is one of the hardest open issues in modern AI: benchmarks shape what models optimize for, and poorly designed benchmarks produce models that are great at benchmarks but useless in practice.

chunks.h: When to Fine-Tune (and When Not To)
chunks.x: You need a specific style, tone, or format consistently across responses. The model's base behavior is inappropriate for your domain (e.g., medical). You have proprietary data that the model should learn from. Latency matters and you want a smaller fine-tuned model that beats a larger prompted one.

chunks.x: You need real-time knowledge, use RAG instead. The behavior you want is achievable via prompting, much cheaper. You don't have at least 1K high-quality examples, quality data is the bottleneck. The model needs to generalize to situations not in your data, prompts generalize better.

chunks.pt: The foam of meaning

chunks.x: This is not a rejection of statistics. It is a change of level of description. The claim is that the most natural and powerful language for describing meaning is the language of spaces, shapes, maps, and invariants — the language of geometry and topology.

chunks.x: Let us begin with the most basic object. Let X be the space of all potential linguistic configurations. An element of X is a linguistic form: a string, a phonological pattern, a syntactic frame, or more generally anything that can be uttered or written. We do not need to fix a precise alphabet or grammar at this stage.…

chunks.pt: The foam of meaning
chunks.x: A topology. There is a natural notion of closeness between linguistic forms. Two forms are close if they differ by a small perturbation — a substitution of a nearby phoneme, a minor syntactic rearrangement, a single-word change. This gives X the structure of a topological space, and often of a metric or pseudometric sp…

chunks.pt: The foam of meaning
chunks.x: A measure. There is a natural notion of typicality or frequency. Some regions of X are densely populated (common phrases, grammatical frames), others are sparse (novel combinations, poetic inversions). This measure is what makes the statistics of language possible, and it is what connects the geometry to observable dat…

chunks.pt: The foam of meaning
chunks.x: A notion of scale. Linguistic structure is visible at every scale: phonemes, morphemes, words, phrases, sentences, discourse, genre. The space X is therefore naturally multi-scale, and the right mathematical language for this is that of fractal or self-similar geometry.

chunks.pt: The foam of meaning
chunks.x: The space X is best thought of as a landscape: a vast, mostly empty terrain, with islands of high density (frequent, conventional utterances), rivers and filaments connecting the islands (productive grammatical patterns), and wide plains or voids (ungrammatical or simply unused regions).

chunks.pt: The foam of meaning
chunks.x: The landscape metaphor is not merely decorative. It is the source of the central vocabulary of this chapter: clusters, filaments, and voids are not analogies borrowed after the fact, but the actual geometric features of X that the theory is designed to detect and explain.

chunks.h: What X is not: a list of vectors
chunks.x: The construction above defines X cleanly, but it may feel remote from the way language is handled in practice. Now that the space is explicit, it helps to say what it is not — and the most important contrast is with the picture that dominates modern practice.

chunks.pt: The foam of meaning
chunks.h: What X is not: a list of vectors
chunks.x: A common modern move is to represent each utterance as a high-dimensional vector — a "word embedding" or a "sentence embedding" — and to do all the geometry in that vector space. We want to be clear about what our X is and is not relative to this.

chunks.pt: The foam of meaning
chunks.h: What X is not: a list of vectors
chunks.x: X is not a fixed list of vectors. There is no finite, canonical basis in which "all of language" is a list of points. The set of possible utterances is (effectively) infinite, and its structure is not linear. A vector-space embedding is a local, learned approximation to a region of X: it flattens a curved patch of the…

chunks.pt: The foam of meaning
chunks.h: What X is not: a list of vectors
chunks.x: X is a space with a geometry of its own. What we mean by this is that the interesting mathematical facts about X are invariant under change of representation. chunks.pt: The foam of meaning
chunks.x: A single binary split between "meaningful" and "meaningless" hides real structure. Once we have the coherence fields, void breaks into four distinct kinds — the four coordinate directions of the void vector.

chunks.pt: The foam of meaning
chunks.x: Syntactic void. The configuration lacks internal syntactic organization. Example: "asdf qwer seven blue because table tomorrow." Here C(x)≈ 0. This is the most straightforward kind of emptiness.

chunks.pt: The foam of meaning
chunks.x: Semantic void. The configuration is syntactically structured but fails to form a stable interpretation. Example: "The thought drinks the square Tuesday." It can have C(x)≈ 1 while S(x)≪ 1 — substantial local structure, but none of the right higher-order relations. High syntactic structure does not force high semantic s…

chunks.pt: The foam of meaning
chunks.x: Grounding void. A structure can be internally coherent and semantically well-specified while having no connection to a world: C(x)≈ 1, S(x)≈ 1, but G(x)≈ 0. A purely formal mathematical system is the limiting example — its relations are perfectly well-defined without its symbols naming anything physical.

chunks.pt: The foam of meaning
chunks.x: Epistemic void. An expression can have a determinate meaning without its truth being known: S(x)≈ 1 does not imply E(x)≈ 1. A proposition may be meaningful but unresolved.

chunks.pt: The foam of meaning
chunks.x: These voids are not necessarily separate regions: the same point can be a void with respect to one structure and a dense region with respect to another. The strongest meaningful region is the intersection of all four, Mₛₜᵣₒₙg = Cₛyₙ ∩ Cₛeₘ ∩ Cgᵣₒᵤₙd ∩ Ceₚᵢ, while weaker forms of meaning occupy the other intersections.

chunks.pt: The foam of meaning

chunks.x: The key point is that voids are not the absence of structure but a part of the structure. The shape of the voids is as meaningful as the shape of the clusters. To map a language space completely is to map both.

chunks.pt: The foam of meaning

chunks.x: Void is a direction, not a place: from the fully-meaningful center, dropping syntax, semantics, grounding, or epistemic determination each leads to a different kind of void.

chunks.pt: The foam of meaning
chunks.x: A semantic phase transition is when a small change in configuration produces a qualitative change in connectivity. The first two sentences above are close and both meaningful; the second and third differ by a single word, yet one is meaningful and the other is not. Meaning can fail abruptly, the way water turns to ice…

chunks.pt: The foam of meaning

chunks.pt: The foam of meaning
chunks.x: Boundaries are where meaning changes. Interior points are tediously uniform. If we want to understand semantics, we must study the boundaries, not the centres.

chunks.x: No finite vocabulary is exact. A rate-distortion bound says the average semantic distortion of a vocabulary of size N scales as N⁻²/k. chunks.x: Here is the theory's sharpest and most testable claim, and the one that links most directly to the Voronoi picture above. Gärdenfors' criterion P says that a natural property — one our language actually uses, like "red" or "near" or "fast" — corresponds to a convex region of a quality domain:

chunks.pt: The foam of meaning
chunks.h: Criterion P: a natural property is a convex region
chunks.x: If two things are red, then every colour between them is red too. Convexity is what makes a property learnable and communicable: you can generalise from a few examples to the whole region, and a shared metric lets two people agree on the boundary without enumerating every member. The claim is not merely plausible; it i…

chunks.pt: The foam of meaning
chunks.h: Criterion P: a natural property is a convex region
chunks.x: Convexity also quietly answers one of the oldest puzzles in the philosophy of induction. Goodman's grue — green before 2030, blue after — fits every emerald we have ever seen as well as "green" does, yet no one induces with it. Geometrically, "green" and "blue" are convex regions of the time–colour space, while "grue"…

chunks.pt: The foam of meaning
chunks.h: Criterion P: a natural property is a convex region
chunks.x: And convexity is where the Voronoi thread pays off. Give each concept a prototype — the central representative, the "best" bird or the "most red" red — and assign every new object to its nearest prototype. The decision regions that fall out are automatically convex, and their shared walls are the familiar Voronoi bound…

chunks.pt: The foam of meaning
chunks.h: Criterion P: a natural property is a convex region
chunks.x: Click to drop examples of a concept. The dashed outline is their convex hull — the smallest convex region containing them. If the concept truly fills that region, it satisfies criterion P and is a natural property; if it only occupies part of it (leaving a hole the hull fills), it is not — "grue" in the flesh.

chunks.pt: The foam of meaning
chunks.h: Criterion P: a natural property is a convex region
chunks.x: The hull is the convex closure of your examples. A natural category coincides with its hull; an artificial one (draw "grue" as a ring) does not — the hull fills a middle the category never occupies.

chunks.pt: The foam of meaning
chunks.x: Language has no single characteristic scale. A handful of words, phrases, and constructions occur very often, while an enormous long tail of forms occurs very rarely. This is the fingerprint of a scale-free, potentially fractal organisation — and it is already an established empirical fact about language.

chunks.x: We now turn to the geometric features of X (and, derivatively, of S). The central claim of this chapter is that a meaningful language space has a characteristic shape, and that the shape is best described by three kinds of feature:

chunks.pt: The foam of meaning
chunks.x: Clusters are regions of X that are densely populated and internally cohesive. They correspond to conventional or frequent linguistic configurations: idioms, collocations, grammatical frames, topic domains. A cluster is a place where many utterances are close to one another and where the interpretation map π is relative…

chunks.pt: The foam of meaning
chunks.x: Filaments are thin, elongated regions of moderate density that connect clusters. They correspond to productive patterns: grammatical operations, constructions, and schemas that allow one to move from one conventional region to another by a regular, rule-like transformation. A filament is a bridge between clusters, and…

chunks.pt: The foam of meaning
chunks.x: Voids are regions of X that are sparsely or not at all populated. They correspond to ungrammatical, infelicitous, or simply unused configurations. A void is not merely "missing data"; it is a meaningful absence. The shape of the voids is as informative as the shape of the clusters, because the voids define the boundari…

chunks.pt: The foam of meaning
chunks.x: Together, clusters, filaments, and voids define the landscape of the language space. The landscape is not uniform: it is a hierarchy of dense regions connected by thin bridges, set against a background of empty space. This is precisely the shape that is observed in other complex, scale-free systems — most famously, the…

chunks.pt: The foam of meaning
chunks.h: Open problems and a research programme
chunks.x: Problem 1 (Existence and construction of X). We have described X as the space of all potential linguistic configurations, but we have not constructed it. What is the precise topological space? A metric space, a simplicial complex, a topos? The answer will determine which invariants are available.

chunks.pt: The foam of meaning

chunks.x: Problem 2 (The interpretation map π). We have treated π as a given. But π is not observed directly; it is inferred. What are the precise constraints that determine π? Is it a morphism in a specific category? The commutativity condition is a start, but it is not a full specification.

chunks.pt: The foam of meaning
chunks.h: Open problems and a research programme
chunks.x: Problem 3 (The heavy tail and meaning). We have claimed that meaning lives in the heavy tail. This needs to be made precise and tested. What is the measurable signature of "meaning in the tail"? Can it be detected in persistent homology, in the geometry of the tail, or in the behavior of π on low-frequency forms?

chunks.pt: The foam of meaning

chunks.pt: The foam of meaning

chunks.x: A neural network is a stack of functions f. A function has a symmetry when some operation on its input changes the input but the output moves in a predictable, structured way. Write a symmetry as σ and its action on an input x as σ · x (here the dot means “apply σ to x,” not multiplication). Two behaviors matter:

chunks.pt: The Shape of the Machine — A Working Geometry for AI
chunks.h: Symmetry: invariance, equivariance, and the shape of attention
chunks.x: Invariant — the output does not change: f(σ · x) = f(x) for a symmetry σ (say, reordering the inputs). The output “forgets” the symmetry. Equivariant — the output changes the same way the input did: f(σ · x) = σ · f(x). The function “commutes” with the symmetry.

chunks.pt: Hyperparameters: The Numbers You Choose

chunks.pt: Inference Optimization
chunks.x: Training a frontier model costs US Dollar 100M+; serving it can cost US Dollar 1M+ per day at scale. Inference optimization makes LLMs economically viable. The frontier in 2025: serving 100+ million tokens per second per cluster with sub-100ms latency.

chunks.pt: Inference Optimization
chunks.x: This chapter covers every lever: quantization, KV-cache management, paged attention, FlashAttention, speculative decoding, batching, distillation, and the serving stacks that tie it together.

chunks.pt: An Intuition of how Large Language Models (LLMs) work
chunks.x: We can think of LLMs as machines that predict the next most likely word, given a context — only one word at a time. That word is appended to the input and fed back in, and the loop repeats until a special token signals the end.

chunks.pt: An Intuition of how Large Language Models (LLMs) work
chunks.x: Computers don't understand words. They understand numbers. So the very first thing an LLM does is chop the input into small pieces called tokens. We can first think of these tokens as words, but they don't have to be. They can be sub-words, numbers, or any part of a text. While we humans think in words, the LLM “thinks…

chunks.pt: An Intuition of how Large Language Models (LLMs) work
chunks.x: Most tokens are common words or word fragments. "understanding" might split into "under" + "standing" — two tokens. That is the quiet genius of it: a word the model has never seen can still be assembled from pieces it knows by heart.

chunks.pt: An Intuition of how Large Language Models (LLMs) work
chunks.x: Where a word splits depends on the data the model was trained on. It chooses that automatically, and once chosen, the vocabulary stays fixed for the life of the model — a fixedness with strange consequences for the rare tokens almost nobody ever trained on (Li et al., 2024).

chunks.pt: An Intuition of how Large Language Models (LLMs) work
chunks.x: Break every unfamiliar word into familiar pieces and nothing is truly new. The vocabulary never has to grow — transformer is just trans + form + er, three pieces the model already knows.

chunks.x: Some tokens are almost never seen in training, so their embeddings stay nearly arbitrary. chunks.x: The most famous example is SolidGoldMagikarp. It is not a word and not a random string: it is the Reddit handle of a user who posted repeatedly in r/counting, a subreddit where people count upward, one number per comment. Such names appeared so often in that corner of the web that the tokenizer gave some of them their…

chunks.pt: An Intuition of how Large Language Models (LLMs) work
chunks.x: That is the lesson in miniature. A token is not a concept the model knows; it is a slot the model had to fill from data. If the slot was filled with almost nothing, there is almost nothing behind it — and what comes out is whatever the surrounding statistics happen to drag along.

chunks.pt: An Intuition of how Large Language Models (LLMs) work
chunks.x: By itself, a number means nothing. So how does “time” come to mean something — and “truth” come to mean something nearby?

chunks.pt: An Intuition of how Large Language Models (LLMs) work
chunks.x: Step 2: Embedding — A raw token tells the model nothing about what a word means. So the model replaces each token with a long list of numbers — a vector — that stands for its meaning.

chunks.x: A raw token tells the model nothing about what a word means. So the model replaces each token with a long list of numbers — a vector — that stands for its meaning.

chunks.pt: An Intuition of how Large Language Models (LLMs) work
An Intuition of how Large Language Models (LLMs) work
chunks.x: These vectors live in a high-dimensional space where words with similar meanings end up close together. To make this tangible, the demo below plots a tiny slice of that space — just two semantic axes the model might discover: Power and Gender. “Man” and “Prince” sit close on the Power axis; “Man” and “Woman” sit close…

chunks.pt: An Intuition of how Large Language Models (LLMs) work
chunks.x: And the space doesn't just capture similarity — it captures relationships. The most famous example:

chunks.pt: An Intuition of how Large Language Models (LLMs) work
chunks.x: The direction from “Man” to “Woman” stands for the concept of gender. Carry that same direction from “King” and you land right next to “Queen.” Nobody typed that rule in — it fell out of the statistics of the text (Word2Vec).

chunks.pt: An Intuition of how Large Language Models (LLMs) work
chunks.x: Real networks don't use two dimensions but thousands — far too many to picture. The principle stays the same: position encodes meaning, direction encodes relationship.

chunks.pt: An Intuition of how Large Language Models (LLMs) work
chunks.x: 💡 Directions encode meaning. The vector Man → Woman points in a direction that's the same wherever you take it — and so does Man → Prince. The model was never taught this — it emerged from the texts themselves.

chunks.pt: An Intuition of how Large Language Models (LLMs) work
chunks.x: Nobody told the model that Man → Woman is the same arrow as King → Queen. The relationship simply is a direction in the space — and arithmetic on directions turns out to be arithmetic on ideas.

chunks.pt: An Intuition of how Large Language Models (LLMs) work
chunks.x: There is still a blind spot: to the model, “dog bites man” and “man bites dog” look exactly the same.

chunks.pt: An Intuition of how Large Language Models (LLMs) work

chunks.pt: An Intuition of how Large Language Models (LLMs) work
chunks.x: “The dog bites man” means something very different from “The man bites dog.” Same words, different order. So a positional encoding is added to each token's embedding — a unique signal that says “I'm the 1st word,” “I'm the 2nd word,” and so on.

chunks.pt: An Intuition of how Large Language Models (LLMs) work
chunks.x: Now each token carries two pieces of information: what it is and where it is. This is not a nicety — the embedding and attention operations have no built-in notion of sequence order, so without it, the two sentences above would be indistinguishable to the model.

chunks.pt: An Intuition of how Large Language Models (LLMs) work
chunks.x: Strip the positional signal out and “dog bites man” and “man bites dog” collapse into the identical, unordered bag of tokens — the same thing to the model, opposite things to you.

chunks.pt: An Intuition of how Large Language Models (LLMs) work
chunks.x: Now every token knows what it is and where it is. But not one of them has spoken to another yet.

chunks.x: This is the heart of the model — the Transformer architecture (Vaswani et al., 2017). The token vectors flow through many layers stacked on top of each other (modern LLMs can have 80+ layers), each one refining the model's understanding a little more.

chunks.pt: An Intuition of how Large Language Models (LLMs) work
chunks.x: Call the vector a token starts with x₀. Every layer adds its output to what is already there instead of overwriting it, so that nothing learned earlier is ever thrown away. If layer l reads hₗ and writes back its own contribution, the rule is:

chunks.pt: An Intuition of how Large Language Models (LLMs) work
chunks.x: In general hₗ₊₁ = hₗ + Layer(hₗ), starting from h₀ = x₀.

chunks.pt: An Intuition of how Large Language Models (LLMs) work
chunks.x: This running vector is called the residual stream. It was originally invented to prevent the vanishing gradient problem, but it also acts as a shared notebook: each layer reads from the notebook, does some thinking, and writes its findings back to it.

Attention allows to find out which word attends to which other word over short or even very long texts, and it can do so over the whole context length of the…

chunks.h: 4a: Attention - “Which other words matter for this word?”
chunks.x: It does so by moving the Embedding of a word in dependence of the context it's used in to a place called contextualized Embedding that looks not only at the word, but at the context the word is used in.

chunks.pt: An Intuition of how Large Language Models (LLMs) work
chunks.h: 4a: Attention - “Which other words matter for this word?”
chunks.x: This is best exemplified when using words that have multiple meanings, like “bank”, which could be a river bank, or a bank where you put your money.

chunks.pt: An Intuition of how Large Language Models (LLMs) work
chunks.h: 4a: Attention - “Which other words matter for this word?”
chunks.x: Cycle through the examples below. Notice how the diamond — the contextualized “Bank” — leaps toward the neighbor that defines it. This is what Attention does: it looks at the context a word is used in, and moves the Embedding of a word in the Embedding Space to a point closer to its meaning in the context it's used in.

chunks.pt: An Intuition of how Large Language Models (LLMs) work
chunks.h: 4a: Attention - “Which other words matter for this word?”
chunks.x: LLM models have many attention heads running in parallel, each a tiny specialist. One might track which noun a pronoun refers to, another might connect verbs to their objects, another might notice adjectives describing nearby nouns.

chunks.pt: An Intuition of how Large Language Models (LLMs) work
chunks.h: 4a: Attention - “Which other words matter for this word?”
chunks.x: It matters, though, that not every head does something a human can read off. A head may look like it reacts to nouns or verbs while in reality it is just a pattern learned from statistics — not programmed to react to those words, and not "knowing" what they are (Elhage et al., 2021).

chunks.pt: An Intuition of how Large Language Models (LLMs) work
chunks.h: 4a: Attention - “Which other words matter for this word?”
chunks.x: “Bank” is not one fixed point. In the context of water it slides toward the river sense; in the context of money, toward finance. Attention does not care how far away the clue is — it reads the context and moves the vector wherever the context points.

chunks.pt: An Intuition of how Large Language Models (LLMs) work
chunks.h: 4a: Attention - “Which other words matter for this word?”
chunks.x: Some heads do have a crisp job a human can name — but many fire on patterns no one would ever write down, and the model works perfectly well anyway. A head is a filter the training process stumbled onto, not a job description written by a designer; even the readable ones are usually understood only after the fact.

chunks.x: After attention has gathered context, a small neural network processes each token on its own. Unlike attention, it does not look at other tokens — it looks at one token's vector and transforms it. In a modern LLM this block holds about two-thirds of all the parameters, which is why most of the model's stored knowledge…

chunks.pt: An Intuition of how Large Language Models (LLMs) work
chunks.x: The usual cartoon says three things happen: pattern detectors fire, a filter zeroes the weak ones, and knowledge is added back. That is a useful first picture — but the modern version is sharper and a little stranger:

chunks.pt: An Intuition of how Large Language Models (LLMs) work
chunks.x: It is a key → value memory. The first matrix holds thousands of keys: patterns in the token's vector. When a key matches, the second matrix writes a value — not a stored sentence, but a distribution over the next tokens that this kind of pattern tends to be followed by. Lower layers key on shallow patterns (word forms,…

chunks.pt: An Intuition of how Large Language Models (LLMs) work
chunks.x: Real neurons are mostly polysemantic — one neuron responds to several unrelated things — because the model packs far more features than it has neurons, a phenomenon called superposition (Elhage et al., 2022). Sparse autoencoders can untangle those activations into features a human can actually read (Bricken et al., 202…

chunks.pt: An Intuition of how Large Language Models (LLMs) work
chunks.x: Let us follow the word “Apple”. Thanks to attention, its vector already carries clues about its context. Depending on whether those clues say eating or buying, a different set of keys matches — and a different value distribution is written into the stream.

chunks.pt: An Intuition of how Large Language Models (LLMs) work
chunks.x: “Apple” is one vector, but a different set of keys matches depending on the company it keeps — and each key writes a different value: pie and juice, or Mac and iPhone. The model did not look a fact up; a pattern matched, and a distribution over the next words shifted.

chunks.pt: An Intuition of how Large Language Models (LLMs) work
chunks.x: And crucially, neither the attention heads nor the feed-forward network are configured by hand. They learn what to look for by looking at massive amounts of data.

chunks.pt: An Intuition of how Large Language Models (LLMs) work
chunks.x: Every layer reads the same running stream — “what the sentence means so far” — thinks for a moment, and writes its finding back, added on top. Eighty layers deep, the original word is still in there. The network is less a pipeline than one shared notebook, passed hand to hand and annotated by everyone.

chunks.pt: The History of Language: From Sanskrit to LLMs
chunks.x: The intelligence of a modern Large Language Model (LLM) is the digital climax of a multi-million-year trajectory. To understand how a machine “speaks,” we must trace the path from the biological re-engineering of the primate throat and the ear that decodes it to the ancient mathematical formalization of grammar.

chunks.pt: Loss: Teaching through Failure
chunks.x: In the previous section, we saw how AI represents data as Tensors. But how does a model actually learn to give the right answer? It uses a Loss Function.

chunks.pt: Loss: Teaching through Failure
chunks.x: A Loss Function is a mathematical way of measuring “how wrong” the AI is. If the AI's guess is far from the truth, the Loss is a high number. If the guess is perfect, the Loss is zero. Training an AI is essentially the process of turning knobs (parameters) to make this Loss number as small as possible.

chunks.pt: Basic Math Concepts II — Linear Algebra for AI
chunks.x: Modern AI is, at its core, applied linear algebra. Every image, every word, every token lives in a high-dimensional vector space. This chapter introduces the mathematical objects that make neural networks possible: vectors, matrices, tensors, and the operations that combine them.

chunks.x: Recall from Math II, the central idea: a vector lives in a space, and operations on vectors (addition, scaling, dot product) correspond to geometric operations on the space. Modern AI happens in vector spaces of dimension 768 to 16,000.

chunks.pt: Basic Math Concepts III — Approximation, High Dimensions & a Taste of Type Theory
chunks.x: For the rest of this chapter, the only fact about vector spaces we need is the following: most vector-space intuition from 2D and 3D fails catastrophically in high dimensions. Understanding the difference is essential to understanding modern AI.

chunks.pt: Basic Math Concepts III — Approximation, High Dimensions & a Taste of Type Theory
chunks.x: Classical statistics warns: as dimensionality grows, geometry breaks down.

chunks.pt: Basic Math Concepts III — Approximation, High Dimensions & a Taste of Type Theory
chunks.x: Distance concentration: in d dimensions, the ratio between the nearest and farthest distance from a point to its k nearest neighbors approaches 1 as d → ∞. All points become roughly equidistant.

chunks.pt: Basic Math Concepts III — Approximation, High Dimensions & a Taste of Type Theory
chunks.x: Volume explosion: the unit cube in d dimensions has volume 1, but almost all of that volume lies in a thin shell near its surface, not in its interior. A uniform sample from the cube is therefore almost surely close to the boundary.

chunks.pt: Basic Math Concepts III — Approximation, High Dimensions & a Taste of Type Theory
chunks.x: Sample complexity: to densely cover a d-dimensional unit cube with samples, you need exponentially many samples as d grows. With d = 100 and 10 samples per axis, you need 10¹⁰⁰ samples, more than atoms in the universe.

chunks.pt: Basic Math Concepts III — Approximation, High Dimensions & a Taste of Type Theory
chunks.x: These are real problems for classical statistical methods. Naïve nearest-neighbor classifiers, density estimators, and clustering algorithms all degrade as d grows.

chunks.pt: Basic Math Concepts III — Approximation, High Dimensions & a Taste of Type Theory
chunks.x: The phrase "curse of dimensionality" comes from dynamic programming, not from a theorem about all high-dimensional data. Bellman used it for the explosion of state spaces: a grid with ten points per axis needs 10^d points in d dimensions (Bellman, 1957; Bellman, 1961). The geometric symptoms are real but distribution-d…

chunks.x: You may have heard of the “curse of dimensionality”: in high dimensions, distance metrics break down, and all points become roughly equidistant. But there is a corresponding blessing of dimensionality that makes neural networks possible.

chunks.pt: Basic Math Concepts III — Approximation, High Dimensions & a Taste of Type Theory
chunks.x: In high-dimensional spaces, random vectors are almost always nearly orthogonal. In 768 dimensions (a typical embedding size), two random vectors have an expected cosine similarity near 0 with small variance, the probability that a cosine has magnitude above 0.1 is only about 0.6\%:

chunks.pt: Basic Math Concepts III — Approximation, High Dimensions & a Taste of Type Theory
chunks.x: This means the model can store thousands of nearly-independent features because high-dimensional space provides exponentially many “almost-orthogonal” directions for free. This is what makes superposition (the ability to represent more features than dimensions) geometrically possible.

chunks.x: And then: when are two 2-paths the same? Answer: a 3-path. And so on, ad infinitum. At every level there are paths-between-paths, and the question of whether those are equal pushes you up one more level. HoTT takes the full infinite tower seriously: an equality is not a single bit, it is an entire ∞-groupoid.

chunks.pt: Mechanistic Interpretability
chunks.h: The FFN as a Soft Hash Table
chunks.x: The columns of W₁ are keys (address patterns). The dot product x W₁ computes the match score between the input x and every key. ReLU zeroes out non-matching keys. chunks.pt: Mechanistic Interpretability
chunks.h: The FFN as a Soft Hash Table
chunks.x: This is exactly a soft hash table: instead of exact-match lookup (hard hashing), the FFN performs approximate-match retrieval where multiple keys can partially match and their values are blended. The “hash function” is the learned projection W₁, and the “hash table entries” are the rows/columns of W₁ and W₂.

chunks.pt: Smallest possible neural network
chunks.x: We previously mentioned initializing weights “randomly.” But “random” is a dangerous word in engineering. If we pick weights from a Uniform Distribution between -1000 and 1000, the signal will explode towards infinity (NaN). If we pick them between -0.0001 and 0.0001, the signal will vanish to zero.

He initialization, designed for ReLU, uses variance 2/nᵢnputs:

chunks.pt: Smallest possible neural network

chunks.pt: Smallest possible neural network
chunks.x: A single neuron computes y = ax + b: one input, one weight, one output. But a Transformer with dₘₒdeₗ = 4096 processes 4096 numbers simultaneously at every step. The bridge between these two scales is the matrix.

chunks.pt: Smallest possible neural network
chunks.x: Instead of computing one neuron at a time, we pack all inputs into a vector x and all weights into a matrix W. The entire layer's computation becomes:

chunks.pt: Smallest possible neural network
chunks.x: This single line represents thousands of individual multiplications and additions, all happening in parallel. Every row of W is a separate “neuron” with its own set of weights. Every row of W receives the same input x. The matrix multiplication Wx computes the dot product of every row with x simultaneously.

chunks.pt: Smallest possible neural network
chunks.x: This is why GPUs are so effective for deep learning: they are designed to perform matrix multiplications in hardware, processing thousands of operations per clock cycle. A modern GPU can execute a 4096 × 4096 matrix times a 4096-dimensional vector, over 16 million individual multiplications, in a single operation. With…

chunks.x: So when you see h = Attention(Q, K, V), remember that every letter in that equation is a matrix, and every operation is a batch of thousands of parallel arithmetic operations, each one as simple as the single neuron y = ax + b.

chunks.pt: AI Music & Video Generation
chunks.x: Simultaneous (spectral) masking: a loud tone makes quieter tones at nearby frequencies inaudible. Play a loud A and a soft B next to it and you stop hearing the B. chunks.pt: Understanding Layer Normalization
chunks.h: Geometric Intuition: LayerNorm as Projection onto a Sphere
chunks.x: LayerNorm has a beautiful geometric interpretation: after centering (subtracting the mean) and normalizing by the standard deviation, the output vector ̂x lies on the surface of a sphere of radius √d in d-dimensional space. The learnable parameters γ and β then stretch and shift this sphere.

chunks.pt: Understanding Layer Normalization
chunks.h: Geometric Intuition: LayerNorm as Projection onto a Sphere
chunks.x: Step 1 - Centering: Subtracting the mean μ shifts the cloud of vectors so that their center of mass is at the origin. This removes the “DC offset”, the shared common signal across all features.

chunks.pt: Understanding Layer Normalization
chunks.h: Geometric Intuition: LayerNorm as Projection onto a Sphere
chunks.x: Step 2 - Normalization: Dividing by the standard deviation σ scales each vector to have length √d. Every vector now lies on the surface of a d-dimensional hypersphere of radius √d. The direction of the vector, the relative pattern of activations, is preserved, but its magnitude is standardized.

chunks.pt: Understanding Layer Normalization
chunks.h: Geometric Intuition: LayerNorm as Projection onto a Sphere
chunks.x: Step 3 - Scale and Shift: The learnable parameters γ (gain) and β (bias) allow the model to deform this sphere: γ stretches or compresses the sphere along each axis (an anisotropic scaling) β shifts the entire sphere away from the origin

chunks.pt: The Optimizer: Navigating the Loss Landscape
chunks.x: This division is the key insight: parameters with large, consistent gradients get smaller effective steps (because √̂vₜ is large), while parameters with small or rare gradients get larger effective steps. The optimizer automatically adapts.

chunks.pt: The Optimizer: Navigating the Loss Landscape

chunks.pt: Production Serving & Inference
chunks.x: Training is once; inference is forever. A frontier LLM might be trained for $100M and then served billions of times at a per-call cost that determines profitability. This chapter covers the systems stack that makes LLM inference fast, cheap, and reliable.

chunks.x: Naïve KV-cache allocation reserves a contiguous block per request: if a request needs 4K tokens but only 2K are used, the rest is wasted. With many requests, fragmentation can waste 30–60% of KV memory.

chunks.pt: Production Serving & Inference
chunks.x: Paged Attention (vLLM) treats the KV cache like OS virtual memory (Kwon et al., 2023):

chunks.pt: Production Serving & Inference
chunks.x: Allocate fixed-size physical blocks (typically 16 tokens each). Each request has a block table mapping logical → physical blocks. Blocks can be shared across requests with the same prefix (e.g., the system prompt). No fragmentation; near-100% memory utilization.

chunks.x: A small, fast draft model (e.g., 1B) generates k candidate tokens autoregressively (fast, ~10× the throughput). chunks.pt: Reinforcement Learning
chunks.x: Reinforcement Learning (RL) is the third pillar of machine learning, alongside supervised and unsupervised learning. In RL, an agent takes actions in an environment to maximize a cumulative reward signal. It is the foundation of modern LLM alignment: RLHF, DPO, GRPO, and the o1/R1 paradigm all build on it.

chunks.pt: Reinforcement Learning
chunks.x: This chapter covers the mathematical core: Markov Decision Processes, value functions, policy gradients, and how modern preference optimization emerged, grouped from the foundations, through policy optimization, to the LLM-preference methods and the open problems that remain.

chunks.pt: Running Models Locally
chunks.x: You don't need a GPU cluster to run a powerful LLM. A quantized 70B model runs on a MacBook. A 7B model in int4 fits on a phone. The local-LLM ecosystem in 2025 is mature enough for serious work: privacy-preserving inference, offline use, fine-tuning on consumer hardware, and even agents that never touch the cloud.

chunks.x: The K-quant schemes (Q2K through Q5K_M) use k-quantization with importance-aware mixed precision: most weights are quantized to the target bits, but sensitive layers get extra bits. IQ-quants (Importance-aware Quantization) push to 1–2 bits with surprisingly good quality.

chunks.x: Given a probability distribution over the next token, which one do you pick? This is the decoding strategy, and it controls the model's “personality”, focused and deterministic, or wild and creative. The frontier in 2025: many subtle techniques beyond temperature and top-k.

chunks.pt: Statistics I — Distributions and Inference
chunks.x: A fundamental rule in machine learning: never evaluate your model on data it has already seen. This is why datasets are split into separate subsets:

chunks.pt: Statistics I — Distributions and Inference
chunks.x: Training Set (typically 70-80%): Used to adjust the model's weights. The model sees this data and learns from it. Validation Set (typically 10-15%): Used to tune hyperparameters (learning rate, architecture choices) and detect overfitting. The model does not learn from this data, but it influences human decisions about…

chunks.pt: Statistics I — Distributions and Inference
chunks.x: Why three sets? If you tune hyperparameters on the validation set, information about the validation set “leaks” into your model choices. You need a third, completely untouched set to get an honest measure of generalization. In small-data regimes (e.g., medical imaging with only hundreds of samples), k-fold cross-valida…

chunks.pt: Statistics I — Distributions and Inference
chunks.x: A model is only as good as the data it is trained on. If the training data contains historical biases, the model will learn and amplify them. This is not a bug in the math, it is a feature of the statistical learning process: the model faithfully reproduces the patterns it observes.

chunks.pt: Statistics I — Distributions and Inference
chunks.x: Historical Bias: The data reflects existing societal inequalities. A hiring model trained on historical hiring data will learn the gender and racial biases present in past decisions. Representation Bias: Certain groups are under-represented in the dataset. A facial recognition system trained mostly on light-skinned fac…

chunks.pt: Statistics I — Distributions and Inference
chunks.x: The technical consequence: Bias in data leads to systematically different performance across subgroups. The model's overall accuracy may look good, but disaggregated by demographic group, it can reveal dramatic disparities. Detecting and mitigating these biases is an active area of research in fairness in machine learn…

chunks.pt: Training Data Curation
chunks.h: The Scale of Modern Training Data
chunks.x: The Chinchilla scaling law (Hoffmann et al., 2022) suggests that for a given compute budget, models are best trained when tokens ≈ 20 × parameters. So a 70B model needs ~1.4T tokens to be “Chinchilla-optimal”; frontier models now train on 10 × that, trading sample efficiency for capability.

chunks.pt: Training Infrastructure
chunks.x: A 70B-parameter model in fp16 takes 140 GB just for the weights. With Adam optimizer states, gradients, and activations, a single training step requires >1 TB of GPU memory. Modern training infrastructure is the art of splitting this across thousands of GPUs while keeping them busy and synchronized.

chunks.x: This chapter covers the core parallelism strategies: data, tensor, pipeline, sequence, and the FSDP/ZeRO families that underpin frontier training.

chunks.pt: Training Infrastructure

chunks.pt: The Untold History of AI I: From the Big Bang to Civilisation
chunks.x: Suppose absolutely nothing exists, no matter, no laws, no logic. Then there are no rules preventing something from arising, because rules are themselves something. A state of absolute nothingness is therefore inherently unstable: without any prohibition, something can emerge.

chunks.pt: The Untold History of AI I: From the Big Bang to Civilisation
chunks.x: Instead of asking “Why something?”, the question becomes: “What could prevent something from existing?” And the answer is: nothing, because nothingness lacks all causal power. Sustaining a void would itself require a kind of rule, which would already be something.
